sections.section_title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia After Cardiac Surgery: Core Concepts and Case Framing
sections.description: This section introduces the clinical problem of thrombocytopenia and thrombosis after cardiopulmonary bypass, using the case to frame why HIT is both common enough to matter and difficult to recognize in postoperative cardiac patients. It provides the essential background on classic HIT and autoimmune HIT needed to understand the rest of the case without drifting into an overly broad review.
subtopics: Why unfractionated heparin is used in cardiac surgery and cardiopulmonary bypass
Expected postoperative platelet count trends after cardiac surgery versus pathologic thrombocytopenia
Epidemiology of HIT in cardiac surgery patients
Immunopathogenesis of classic HIT: PF4, heparin, IgG antibodies, and FcγRIIa-mediated platelet activation
Thrombotic risk in HIT and why thrombocytopenia paradoxically signals hypercoagulability
Definition and distinguishing biology of autoimmune HIT (aHIT)
Clinical clues that suggest aHIT rather than typical HIT: profound thrombocytopenia, persistence, heparin-independent activation, severe consumptive coagulopathy
Why this case is notable: early onset, ischemic stroke, severe platelet nadir, and unusual serologic behavior

sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Early Diagnostic Suspicion
sections.description: This section reconstructs the patient’s timeline from preoperative exposure through postoperative deterioration, emphasizing how careful chronology led clinicians from an initially nonspecific postoperative platelet fall to concern for HIT. It teaches how to interpret timing, severity, and associated thrombosis in context.
subtopics: Baseline patient factors: age, atrial fibrillation, apixaban use, and structural heart disease
Preoperative heart catheterization and the importance of even small heparin exposures
Cardiac operation details: valve replacement, ascending aortic grafting, CABG, and intraoperative UFH during CPB
Immediate postoperative course and usual LMWH thromboprophylaxis
Platelet count trajectory from preoperative baseline through POD1-POD6
How to distinguish expected CPB-associated platelet decline from progressive HIT-related thrombocytopenia
Neurologic change in the postoperative period: delirium versus occult focal ischemia
Recognition of arterial thrombosis in HIT: interpretation of the parietal stroke in this case
Clinical significance of early-onset HIT after recent heparin exposure
Bedside estimation of pretest probability using timing, thrombocytopenia, thrombosis, and alternative explanations

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis and Laboratory Confirmation of Autoimmune HIT
sections.description: This section explains the structured evaluation of severe post-cardiac surgery thrombocytopenia and shows how competing diagnoses were excluded. It then walks through the interpretation of HIT testing, especially the atypical serotonin-release assay profile that ultimately established autoimmune HIT.
subtopics: Differential diagnosis of severe thrombocytopenia after cardiac surgery
Common postoperative causes to consider: hemodynamic instability, infection, bleeding, dilutional loss, and CPB-related consumption
Rare but important alternatives: post-transfusion purpura, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia, and other thrombotic microangiopathies
Role of CBC trend, hemoglobin stability, white blood cell count, coagulation studies, fibrinogen, hemolysis markers, renal/liver function, cultures, and chest imaging
Peripheral smear interpretation: absence of platelet clumping and initial lack of schistocytes
Use and limitations of PF4/polyanion ELISA in postoperative cardiac patients
Interpretation of a strongly positive ELISA optical density and how OD strength affects diagnostic confidence
Principles of the serotonin-release assay (SRA) and standard heparin-dependent HIT pattern
Key SRA findings in this case: strong activation at low heparin concentrations, no activation at high heparin concentration, and activation even at 0 U/mL heparin
Why heparin-independent platelet activation supports autoimmune HIT
Meaning of incomplete inhibition by Fc receptor-blocking monoclonal antibody IV.3
How an initially 'indeterminate' functional assay can still be diagnostic when integrated with clinical and serologic context
Diagnostic synthesis: linking early onset to preoperative heparin exposure and confirming severe aHIT

sections.section_title: Management Strategy in Severe Autoimmune HIT with Stroke
sections.description: This section focuses on treatment decisions, explaining why all heparin products were stopped, why argatroban and intravenous immunoglobulin were chosen initially, and why therapy was escalated to fondaparinux with antithrombin support. It highlights the challenge of treating a highly prothrombotic disorder in a patient with recent cerebral infarction and profound thrombocytopenia.
subtopics: Immediate principles of HIT treatment: stop all heparin exposure and begin non-heparin anticoagulation
Why prophylactic fondaparinux was insufficient once HIT-associated thrombosis was recognized
Choice of argatroban as initial therapeutic anticoagulant: mechanism, monitoring, advantages, and bleeding considerations
PTT-guided dosing and practical issues in the postoperative setting
Rationale for high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin in autoimmune HIT
Mechanistic basis of IVIG: interruption of Fc receptor-mediated platelet activation
Expected platelet response to IVIG in aHIT and why a blunted response in this case signaled unusually severe disease
Use of serial fibrinogen and D-dimer as markers of ongoing HIT-associated hypercoagulability
Interpretation of falling fibrinogen, rising D-dimer, and later schistocytosis as evidence of consumptive coagulopathy
Reasons for switching from argatroban to therapeutic-dose fondaparinux
Mechanism of fondaparinux and its off-label role in HIT
Importance of antithrombin for fondaparinux efficacy and rationale for AT concentrate supplementation
Balancing thrombosis prevention against hemorrhagic risk after ischemic stroke and major surgery
Supportive management and multidisciplinary coordination among hematology, surgery, neurology, and laboratory medicine

sections.section_title: Recovery, Serologic Evolution, and Clinical Lessons
sections.description: This section follows the patient’s outcome and uses it to teach how autoimmune HIT can evolve over time clinically and in the laboratory. It concludes with the major take-home lessons for learners about recognition, diagnostic reasoning, and prevention of missed or delayed diagnosis in postoperative patients.
subtopics: Platelet count recovery timeline and neurological outcome
Transition from fondaparinux back to long-term apixaban
Persistence of HIT antibodies for months and implications for follow-up testing
Evolution of SRA patterns from heparin-independent activation toward a more typical heparin-dependent profile
How waning antibody behavior supports the diagnosis of autoimmune HIT
Why the absence of a better competing diagnosis mattered in final diagnostic confirmation
Clinical hallmarks of severe aHIT illustrated by this case: early onset, profound nadir, stroke, consumptive coagulopathy, and partial resistance to Fc receptor blockade
Pitfalls in postoperative cardiac surgery patients: over-attributing thrombocytopenia to CPB or delirium to routine postoperative confusion
Practical lessons for recognizing recent heparin exposure outside the operating room
How atypical functional assay results should prompt expert review rather than premature exclusion of HIT
Implications of this novel serologic phenotype for future diagnosis and research
High-yield teaching points and an approach algorithm for suspected HIT/aHIT after cardiac surgery
